::: {.lead}
On the first day of a new job at a game studio, a junior tester gets an
account, a cloud folder and a long list of files. After one week, some files
are lost, two have the name `final.docx`, and one project folder was deleted
by mistake. Every digital task starts with two questions: *who am I for the
system?* and *where is my work stored?* In this lab session you answer both:
you sign in with your university account, build a folder structure for your
courses, name files well, and learn how cloud storage protects your work, and
when it does not. Every section ends with a task on the lab computer.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary account authentication single-sign-on file folder file-path file-extension file-size cloud-storage synchronization backup >}}

## 2.1 Your account and single sign-on

An **account** is how a service knows its user. It has a name (often an
e-mail address), a way to prove who you are, and your data and permissions.
All your accounts and the information in them form your **digital identity**.

**Authentication** means proving that you are the owner of an account.
Systems use three kinds of proof, called *factors*:

- something you **know**: a password or a PIN;
- something you **have**: a phone that gets a code, a security key;
- something you **are**: a fingerprint or a face.

Two different factors together are called **multi-factor authentication
(MFA)**. Week 3 studies it in detail.

A university has many services: e-mail, the e-learning platform, cloud
storage, office apps, the library. Most universities use **single sign-on
(SSO)**: you sign in once with your university account, and all connected
services trust you (@fig-sso).

![Single sign-on: one sign-in with the university account opens several services.](images/sso.png){#fig-sso width=84%}

SSO is easy and safe, because one strong password is easier to protect than
ten weak ones. But it also has a risk: a person who steals your university
password can open *every* service. So good habits on **shared lab
computers** are important:

- sign out of every service, and of the browser, at the end of the session;
- never let the browser save your password on a shared computer;
- use a private (incognito) window on someone else's device;
- lock the screen when you leave, even for one minute (Windows key + L).

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Closing the browser window and thinking you are signed out. On many
computers, the browser keeps you signed in. Always press **Sign out** first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · One sign-in, many services"}
1. Sign in to the lab computer and to your university account in the browser.
2. Open the e-mail, the e-learning platform and the cloud storage, one after
   another. Count the times you had to type your password.
3. At the end of the lab, sign out of the account and close the browser.
   Lock the screen with Windows key + L when you leave your desk.

*Your result:* the list of services you opened, and how many times you typed
your password.
:::

## 2.2 Files, folders and paths

A **file** is a named piece of data in storage: a document, a picture, a
program. A **folder** holds files and other folders. Folders can hold
folders, so the storage of a computer is a **tree**: one top folder branches
into folders, which branch again, down to the files (@fig-tree).

![A folder tree for course work. The highlighted path leads from the top folder to one file.](images/folder-tree.png){#fig-tree width=86%}

The **path** of a file is its address in the tree: the folders from the top
down to the file. Windows separates the folders with `\` and starts with a
drive letter. Mac, Android and web addresses use `/`.

| System | Example path |
|---|---|
| Windows | `C:\Users\Sara\Documents\Courses\Digital-Skills\week-01\cv.docx` |
| Mac | `/Users/sara/Documents/Courses/Digital-Skills/week-01/cv.docx` |
| cloud (in the browser) | `My files > Courses > Digital-Skills > week-01 > cv.docx` |

: The same file on different systems. {#tbl-paths}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Path"}
The **path** of a file is its full address: the folders from the top of the
tree down to the file, and then the file name. Two files can have the same
name, but never the same path.
:::

The part of a file name after the last dot is the **file extension**. It
tells the computer which program opens the file (@fig-types).

![Common file types and the units of file size.](images/file-types.png){#fig-types width=92%}

| Extension | Type | Program |
|---|---|---|
| `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.txt` | documents | Word, a PDF reader, a text editor |
| `.xlsx`, `.csv` | spreadsheets, tables | Excel |
| `.pptx` | presentations | PowerPoint |
| `.png`, `.jpg`, `.svg` | pictures | a picture viewer or editor |
| `.mp3`, `.mp4` | sound, video | a media player |
| `.zip` | a packed archive | the file manager |
| `.exe`, `.apk` | programs, apps | the system: only from trusted sources |

: Common file extensions. {#tbl-ext}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Trusting the icon instead of the extension. Windows hides extensions, so a
dangerous file called `invoice.pdf.exe` looks like `invoice.pdf`, with a
document icon. Showing file extensions is one of the easiest safety settings.
:::

The size of a file is measured in **bytes**. Each unit is 1024 times the
unit before it: 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB and
1 TB = 1024 GB. Windows, and so the lab computer, counts in this way. A short
document is a few KB, a photo a few MB, a video often hundreds of MB. The
e-learning platform and e-mail limit the size of what you can upload.
Makers of USB sticks and phones count in steps of 1000, so a "64 GB" USB
stick shows a little less in Windows (about 60 GB).

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — Will the trailer upload?"}
A student made a game trailer of 2 GB. The e-learning platform accepts files
of 500 MB at most.

1. Change GB to MB: 2 GB = 2 × 1024 MB = 2048 MB.
2. Compare: 2048 MB is more than 500 MB, so the upload fails.
3. Solution: upload the video to your cloud storage and hand in a link, or
   make a shorter video.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/path-finder.html" poster="sims/path-finder.png" title="Path Finder: files, folders and paths" kind="game" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Extensions, sizes and paths"}
1. Open **File Explorer**. Turn on file extensions: View → Show → File name
   extensions (Windows 11), or View → File name extensions (Windows 10).
2. Open the Documents folder. Switch to the **Details** view. Write the
   extension and the size of three files.
3. Right-click one file and choose **Copy as path**. Paste the path into a
   document.
4. Play stages 1 and 2 of **Path Finder** (above).

*Your result:* three files with extension and size, one path, and your Path
Finder score.
:::

## 2.3 Naming and organising files

A file that you cannot find is as good as lost. Professionals follow four
rules for **file names**:

1. **Say what it is**, in the same pattern every time.
2. **No spaces or special characters** (`/ \ : * ? " < > |`). Use `-` or `_`.
3. **Write dates as year-month-day** (2026-10-21), so that sorting by name is
   also sorting by date.
4. **Number the versions** (`v01`, `v02`), not `final`, `final2`,
   `final-really`.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — Better file names"}
| Poor name | Better name |
|---|---|
| `New Document (3).docx` | `2026-10-21_DS_week01_cv_v01.docx` |
| `final final.pptx` | `2026-11-12_pitch-deck_v03.pptx` |
| `IMG_4821.jpg` | `2026-10-21_lab-desk-photo.jpg` |

Sorted by name, the better names are also in date order, and each name says
the course, the week, the content and the version.
:::

Folders need the same care. A good folder tree is short (not more than four
levels), follows the way you work, and has the same shape for every project.
@fig-tree shows a tree for this diploma: one folder for each course, one for
each week.

A game studio usually sorts a project by *kind of content*: `docs` for the
plans, `art` for pictures and models, `audio` for music and sounds, `builds`
for the versions that testers use, and `archive` for old material. Everyone
knows where to look, and a new team member finds their way on the first day.

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Build your course folders"}
In your university cloud storage:

1. Create the folder `Courses`, and in it one folder for each of your four
   courses (for example `Digital-Skills`).
2. In `Digital-Skills`, create `week-01`.
3. Upload your DigComp profile from lesson 1 into `week-01`, and rename it
   with the rules above, for example `2026-10-21_DS_week01_digcomp-profile_v01.pdf`.

*Your result:* the folder tree and the file with a good name.
:::

## 2.4 Cloud storage, synchronization and backup

**Cloud storage** keeps your files on the servers of a company, usually
Microsoft OneDrive or Google Drive for a university. You can open them from
any device after signing in. Advantages: access from everywhere, easy sharing
(week 2), and no loss when one device breaks. Limits: a storage limit (a
**quota**), the need for Internet, and the rules of the company.

**Synchronization** keeps the same files on several devices and in the cloud:
a change on the lab computer appears on your phone a few seconds later. But
synchronization is not the same as **backup** (@fig-sync-backup).

![Synchronization copies every change everywhere, also mistakes. A backup is a separate copy that a mistake does not reach.](images/sync-backup.png){#fig-sync-backup width=90%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.2 — Synchronization and backup"}
**Synchronization** makes several copies the same. If you delete or damage a
file in one place, it is deleted or damaged in all places. A **backup** is a
*separate* copy that you keep to get your data back after a loss, a mistake or
an attack.
:::

Many cloud services have a **recycle bin** and a **version history**. They
keep deleted files and older versions for some time. They help, but they are
not a real backup. A simple rule is the **3-2-1 rule**: keep **3** copies of
important work, on **2** different kinds of storage, with **1** copy in
another place.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — A deleted project folder"}
A student keeps a game project in a synchronized cloud folder and deletes it
by mistake on the lab computer.

1. Synchronization deletes it on the laptop and the phone within seconds.
2. The cloud recycle bin still has it for a limited time (often 30 days). The
   student can restore it, if they notice in time.
3. With the 3-2-1 rule (for example a weekly copy on a USB drive at home), the
   project would be safe even after the recycle bin is emptied.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Versions, delete and restore"}
Use the file from the previous task.

1. Change something in the file (or upload a new copy), and rename it to
   `v02`. Open its **version history** and find the older version.
2. Delete the file. Open the **recycle bin** of the cloud storage and restore
   it. Check that it is back in `week-01`.

*Your result:* one sentence: where did you find the older version, and how
long does your recycle bin keep files?
:::

## Further reading

Evans, Martin and Poatsy, *Technology in Action*, 18th ed., the chapters on
using the Internet and cloud services, and on file management.

## Exercises

1. Name the three kinds of authentication factor, with one example each.
2. What is single sign-on? Give one advantage and one risk.
3. Write four safe habits for shared lab computers.
4. Write the path of `notes.docx` in the folder `week-02` of `Digital-Skills`,
   inside `Courses`, inside `Documents` of the user `ali`, on a Mac.
5. Which program opens each file: `budget.xlsx`, `trailer.mp4`,
   `levels.zip`, `logo.svg`?
6. Why is `photo.jpg.exe` dangerous? Which setting helps you see it?
7. A screen recording of a bug is 3 GB. How many MB is it? Can you send it
   by e-mail with a limit of 25 MB?
8. Rename `My Project FINAL (2).pptx`, made on 3 November 2026 for the Digital
   Skills pitch, with the rules of section 2.3.
9. Why is synchronization not a backup? What is the 3-2-1 rule?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Know (a password), have (a phone with a code), are (a fingerprint).
2. One sign-in opens all connected services. Advantage: one strong password. Risk: a stolen password opens everything.
3. Sign out; do not save passwords; use a private window; lock the screen.
4. `/Users/ali/Documents/Courses/Digital-Skills/week-02/notes.docx`.
5. Excel (a spreadsheet); a media player; the file manager (an archive); a picture viewer or a browser.
6. It is a program that looks like a picture. Turn on "File name extensions".
7. 3 × 1024 MB = 3072 MB. No: it is far more than 25 MB. Share a link from the cloud storage instead.
8. For example `2026-11-03_DS_pitch-deck_v01.pptx`.
9. Synchronization copies deletions and damage to every copy; a backup is separate. 3 copies, on 2 kinds of storage, 1 in another place.
:::
